Uses: infiltration anaesthesia and nerve block for minor surgery and dental work, usually with adrenaline to prolong the effect; as procaine penicillin, where salt formation gives a long-acting depot injection. It is not effective as a surface anaesthetic because it penetrates mucous membranes poorly.
Drawbacks: short duration because plasma pseudocholinesterase hydrolyses it quickly, and hypersensitivity caused by its p-aminobenzoic acid metabolite; a patient allergic to it can be given an amide such as lignocaine.

questions.question: Write the synthesis of benzocaine and explain why it is used only as a surface anaesthetic.
questions.answer:
Synthesis: (1) p-Nitrotoluene is oxidised with potassium dichromate and sulphuric acid, or with alkaline potassium permanganate, to p-nitrobenzoic acid. (2) The nitro group is reduced with tin or iron and hydrochloric acid, or by catalytic hydrogenation, giving p-aminobenzoic acid. (3) Fischer esterification with excess ethanol and a small amount of concentrated sulphuric acid under reflux gives ethyl p-aminobenzoate; the mixture is poured into water, neutralised with sodium carbonate, and the solid is filtered and recrystallised from dilute ethanol. The melting point of the pure product is about 90 degrees Celsius.
Why surface use only: benzocaine has an aromatic ring and an ester link but no basic aliphatic amine, so it cannot be protonated and cannot form a water-soluble salt suitable for injection. It is almost insoluble in water, so it stays where it is applied and is absorbed slowly, and its action depends on the unionised molecule entering the nerve endings directly beneath the surface.
Uses: creams, gels, lozenges, sprays and dusting powders for painful mouth and throat conditions, for ulcers, and on wounds, burns and haemorrhoids.
Caution: excessive application, particularly in infants, has been associated with methaemoglobinaemia.

questions.question: Write the synthesis of tolbutamide and explain the mechanism of action of sulphonylureas.
questions.answer:
Synthesis: (1) Toluene is treated with chlorosulphonic acid, which gives p-toluenesulphonyl chloride. (2) Treatment with ammonia converts the sulphonyl chloride to p-toluenesulphonamide. (3) The sulphonamide is deprotonated with a base such as sodium hydroxide or sodium methoxide and treated with n-butyl isocyanate; the sulphonamide nitrogen adds across the isocyanate carbon-nitrogen double bond to form the sulphonylurea. (4) Acidification precipitates tolbutamide, which is recrystallised. An alternative route condenses p-toluenesulphonamide with n-butylamine through a urethane or carbamate intermediate.
Mechanism: sulphonylureas bind the SUR1 subunit of the ATP-sensitive potassium channel in the membrane of the pancreatic beta cell. The channel closes, so potassium cannot leave; the membrane depolarises, voltage-gated calcium channels open, intracellular calcium rises and insulin-containing granules are released by exocytosis. The effect is independent of blood glucose, which is why hypoglycaemia can occur. Long-term treatment also appears to reduce hepatic insulin clearance and improve tissue sensitivity. Because stored insulin is required, these drugs are ineffective in type 1 diabetes and in advanced beta cell failure.
Note on tolbutamide: its para methyl group is readily oxidised in the liver, so it is short acting and comparatively safe in the elderly.

questions.question: Write the synthesis of dibucaine and compare ester and amide local anaesthetics.
questions.answer:
Synthesis of dibucaine (cinchocaine): (1) 2-Hydroxycinchoninic acid, that is 2-hydroxyquinoline-4-carboxylic acid, is the starting material. (2) Treatment with phosphorus oxychloride or phosphorus pentachloride converts the 2-hydroxyl to a chlorine and the carboxyl group to an acid chloride, giving 2-chloroquinoline-4-carbonyl chloride. (3) Reaction with 2-diethylaminoethylamine forms the carboxamide at position 4. (4) Heating with sodium n-butoxide displaces the chlorine at position 2 by a butoxy group, giving dibucaine, which is converted to the hydrochloride for solutions. It is the most potent and most toxic of the group and is used mainly for surface and spinal anaesthesia.
Comparison:
(1) Chemistry: esters carry a -COO- link, amides an -NHCO- link.
(2) Metabolism: esters are hydrolysed rapidly by plasma pseudocholinesterase and tissue esterases; amides are metabolised slowly by liver microsomal enzymes, so their effect is prolonged in liver disease.
(3) Duration: esters are generally short acting, amides longer acting.
(4) Allergy: esters yield p-aminobenzoic acid, a recognised allergen, so hypersensitivity is relatively common; amides rarely cause allergy, and a patient sensitive to an ester can be given an amide.
(5) Stability: amide solutions are more stable to heat and can be autoclaved, whereas ester solutions hydrolyse on storage.
(6) Examples: esters - cocaine, procaine, benzocaine, tetracaine; amides - lignocaine, mepivacaine, prilocaine, etidocaine, dibucaine.

questions.question: Explain the mechanism of action of metformin and alpha-glucosidase inhibitors, and give their adverse effects.
questions.answer:
Metformin: a biguanide, a small very polar molecule. It activates AMP-activated protein kinase in the liver and muscle, which reduces gluconeogenesis and hepatic glucose output, increases glucose uptake and use by muscle, reduces fatty acid oxidation and slightly reduces appetite and intestinal glucose absorption. It does not stimulate insulin release, so used alone it does not cause hypoglycaemia and it does not cause weight gain; some insulin must nevertheless be present for it to work. It is the first-choice drug in type 2 diabetes, especially in overweight patients, and is also used in polycystic ovary syndrome.
Adverse effects of metformin: metallic taste, anorexia, nausea and diarrhoea, which usually settle if the dose is increased slowly; impaired vitamin B12 absorption on long use; and the rare but potentially fatal lactic acidosis. It is therefore avoided in renal impairment, severe hepatic disease, heart failure with poor perfusion, hypoxic states and alcoholism, and is withheld before procedures using iodinated contrast media and before major surgery.
Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors: acarbose and voglibose are carbohydrate-like molecules that competitively inhibit the alpha-glucosidase enzymes of the intestinal brush border, so disaccharides and oligosaccharides are split more slowly and glucose enters the blood gradually. The peak after a meal is reduced. They act locally and are hardly absorbed, so they do not cause hypoglycaemia alone, and they must be taken with the first mouthful of food.
Adverse effects: flatulence, abdominal cramps, borborygmi and diarrhoea, from carbohydrate fermented by colonic bacteria; rarely raised liver enzymes. Important practical point: if a patient on one of these drugs together with a sulphonylurea or insulin becomes hypoglycaemic, glucose must be given, since sucrose cannot be hydrolysed while the enzyme is inhibited.

questions.question: Why is a local anaesthetic less effective in inflamed tissue, and why is adrenaline added to its solution?
questions.answer: Inflamed tissue is acidic. A local anaesthetic is a weak base, so in an acidic environment most of it exists as the ionised cation, which cannot cross the lipid nerve membrane; too little free base penetrates to the axon and the block is poor. Adrenaline is added because it constricts local blood vessels, so the drug is removed more slowly from the site. This keeps a higher concentration at the nerve, prolongs the block, reduces bleeding in the operative field and lowers the peak blood level and thus systemic toxicity. It must not be used in areas supplied by end arteries such as fingers, toes, ears, nose and penis.

questions.question: What is the chemical difference between rapid-acting insulin analogues and regular insulin, and why does it matter?
questions.answer: Regular soluble insulin molecules associate into zinc-containing hexamers in the vial and in the subcutaneous depot, and these must dissociate into monomers before absorption, which delays the onset by about half an hour. In rapid-acting analogues a few amino acids near the end of the B chain are exchanged or reversed, for example the proline and lysine at B28 and B29 in insulin lispro, which weakens the forces holding the hexamer together. The analogue therefore dissociates at once, is absorbed within minutes and can be injected immediately before or even just after a meal, giving better control of the rise in glucose after eating and a lower risk of late hypoglycaemia.
